title: Why Does My Dog Lick the Air? Normal Reasons, Warning Signs and What to Do
summary: Learn why dogs lick the air, how to tell a harmless scent or excitement response from nausea, dental pain, compulsive behavior or a problem that needs veterinary care.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog lick the air
secondaryKeywords: when to see vet for air licking
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog briefly licking the air while its owner calmly observes the behavior at home
content:
Air licking can be completely harmless, but the pattern matters. A dog may briefly lick the air while smelling something interesting, anticipating food, enjoying a scratch, or responding to excitement. Repeated episodes can also occur with nausea, mouth discomfort, anxiety, compulsive behavior, or less commonly a neurologic problem. The most useful response is to notice what happens immediately before, during, and after the licking instead of assuming one cause.

Quick Answer

If your dog licks the air only for a few seconds in predictable situations and otherwise acts normal, monitor the behavior. Record a short video if it repeats. Check for drooling, lip smacking, repeated swallowing, bad breath, pawing at the mouth, vomiting, appetite change, facial twitching, staring, or difficulty settling. Persistent, increasing, painful, or unusual air licking deserves veterinary evaluation, especially when it appears suddenly.

What Does Air Licking Look Like?

Air licking usually means the tongue repeatedly extends without making obvious contact with food, skin, or another surface. Some dogs make one or two quick tongue movements; others lick rhythmically for minutes. It can be confused with lip licking, which often happens closer to the lips and muzzle. Describing the exact movement helps because different patterns can point toward different triggers.

Common Reasons Dogs Lick the Air

1. Smelling and Processing an Interesting Scent

Dogs experience the world primarily through scent. Brief tongue movements may accompany intense sniffing as the dog investigates odor molecules in the environment. This is more likely to be normal when the dog is relaxed, curious, and easily redirected.

2. Anticipation of Food

Some dogs lick the air when they hear a food bag, watch a meal being prepared, or expect a treat. If the licking begins only around food and stops afterward, learned anticipation is a reasonable explanation. Keep the distinction between normal anticipation and repeated licking with nausea signs in mind.

3. Enjoyment During Petting or Scratching

A few dogs make tongue movements when a favorite spot is scratched. If the body is loose, the dog seeks more contact, and the behavior stops when petting stops, it may simply be an individual response to pleasant stimulation.

4. Nausea or Gastrointestinal Discomfort

Nausea can produce lip licking, air licking, repeated swallowing, drooling, restlessness, grass seeking, or reduced interest in food. A dog that licks the air while pacing, swallowing repeatedly, or looking uncomfortable should be observed more carefully. Vomiting, diarrhea, a swollen abdomen, severe weakness, or repeated unproductive retching requires prompt veterinary attention.

5. Dental or Mouth Pain

A painful tooth, gum disease, an oral injury, or material caught around a tooth can change tongue movements. Clues include bad breath, drooling, chewing on one side, dropping food, reluctance to eat hard food, rubbing the face, or pawing at the mouth. Do not force the mouth open if your dog is painful or defensive.

6. Stress, Arousal, or a Learned Habit

Licking can be a self-soothing behavior. Some dogs begin licking during conflict, uncertainty, overstimulation, or repeated stressful routines. If the behavior has been accidentally reinforced with attention, it may also become a learned response. Look at the whole body: tucked posture, repeated yawning, panting, pacing, avoidance, or inability to settle make stress more likely.

7. Compulsive or Neurologic Causes

Very repetitive air licking that is difficult to interrupt can occasionally be part of a compulsive pattern or neurologic event. Facial twitching, staring, sudden behavior arrest, snapping at invisible objects, confusion, or unusual movements should be recorded on video and discussed with a veterinarian. A video can be far more useful than trying to describe a brief episode from memory.

A Simple Pattern Check at Home

  1. Write down the time and what happened immediately before the licking.
  2. Note whether food, petting, a strong smell, travel, stress, or rest preceded the episode.
  3. Record how long it lasts and whether your dog responds normally to you.
  4. Look for drooling, swallowing, vomiting, mouth discomfort, or appetite changes.
  5. Take a clear video if the behavior repeats.

What Not to Do

Do not punish air licking. Punishment can add stress without addressing nausea, pain, or another underlying cause. Do not give human antacids, anti-nausea medication, pain medicine, or sedatives unless a veterinarian has specifically instructed you to use a product and dose for your dog.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Arrange an examination if air licking is new and frequent, increasing, occurring with poor appetite, bad breath, mouth pain, vomiting, diarrhea, repeated swallowing, weight loss, or obvious distress. Seek urgent care if your dog has difficulty breathing, collapses, has repeated unproductive retching with abdominal enlargement, may have swallowed a toxin or foreign object, or shows a prolonged abnormal neurologic episode.

Related Virixoo Guides

If the movement is mainly around the lips, read Why Does My Dog Keep Licking His Lips?. For excessive saliva, see Why Is My Dog Drooling So Much?.

How to Separate a Brief Habit From a Persistent Problem

Frequency and recovery are especially useful. A dog that gives two tongue flicks after smelling a treat and immediately returns to normal is very different from a dog that spends several minutes licking, swallowing, pacing, or staring. Keep a simple log for three to five days. Record meals, treats, medications, car travel, stressful events, bowel movements, vomiting, and the approximate time of each episode. Patterns around meals may support a gastrointestinal discussion; patterns during handling or social pressure may suggest arousal; episodes with facial movements or altered awareness deserve quicker medical review.

What a Veterinarian May Check

The examination may include the teeth, gums, tongue, roof of the mouth, throat, abdomen, skin, and neurologic responses. Depending on the history, further testing may be recommended. The goal is not to label every lick as disease, but to rule out pain and illness before treating repetitive behavior as purely behavioral.

A Practical Decision Guide

PatternMore Likely Next Step
Brief licking around food, dog otherwise normalMonitor and look for a predictable trigger
Licking plus drooling or repeated swallowingDiscuss nausea or oral discomfort with a veterinarian
Licking plus bad breath or difficulty chewingArrange an oral and dental examination
Long repetitive episodes that are hard to interruptRecord video and seek veterinary assessment
Licking with facial twitching or altered awarenessPrompt veterinary evaluation

FAQ

Why does my dog lick the air after eating?

A few licks can reflect taste, anticipation, or normal mouth movements. Repeated licking with swallowing, drooling, discomfort, or vomiting can be associated with nausea or oral discomfort and should be discussed with a veterinarian if it persists.

Why does my dog lick the air when I scratch him?

Some dogs appear to make tongue movements in response to pleasant stimulation. It is usually less concerning when the dog is relaxed and the licking stops when the scratching stops.

Can air licking be anxiety?

Yes, repetitive licking can occur during stress or overarousal, but medical causes should not be dismissed simply because the dog is anxious.

Should I film the behavior?

Yes. A clear video showing the face and body can help a veterinarian distinguish licking, swallowing, facial movements, and changes in awareness.

Trusted References

PetMD: Why Do Dogs Lick the Air? · PetMD: Canine Compulsive Disorder

title: Why Is My Dog’s Nose Dry? What It Means and When to Worry
summary: A dry dog nose is not automatically a sign of illness. Learn normal causes, what changes matter more than moisture alone, safe care steps, and when a veterinarian should check it.
primaryKeyword: why is my dog's nose dry
secondaryKeywords: when to see vet dry dog nose
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Close view of a healthy dog nose while an owner gently checks for dryness or cracking
content:
A dry nose by itself is a poor test of whether a dog is sick. Dogs can have a warm or dry nose after sleeping, spending time near indoor heating, being outside in dry weather, or simply because they have not licked the nose recently. What matters more is whether the nose is persistently cracked, crusted, painful, bleeding, losing pigment, or accompanied by changes in appetite, energy, breathing, hydration, or behavior.

Quick Answer

If your dog’s nose is temporarily dry but the surface looks intact and your dog is eating, drinking, breathing, and behaving normally, monitor it. Offer normal access to fresh water and move away from extreme heat or dry airflow. Do not apply random human lotions. Contact a veterinarian for persistent crusting, deep cracks, sores, bleeding, swelling, significant color or texture changes, or a dry nose accompanied by illness signs.

Why Dog Noses Are Often Wet

Nasal moisture varies through the day. Dogs lick their noses, nasal tissues produce moisture, and environmental humidity influences how wet the surface feels. A dog may therefore switch between a cool wet nose and a warm dry nose without anything being wrong.

Common Normal Reasons for a Dry Nose

Sleep

Dogs do not lick their noses while asleep. A dry nose immediately after a nap can become moist again after the dog wakes, drinks, moves around, and resumes normal licking.

Dry Indoor Air

Heating, air conditioning, fireplaces, fans, and low humidity can dry exposed skin. Dogs that sleep near vents may show more obvious dryness.

Weather and Sun Exposure

Wind, cold air, hot weather, and sunlight can affect the nose surface. Pale or lightly pigmented noses may be more vulnerable to sun damage. Ask your veterinarian about pet-safe protection rather than applying human sunscreen without guidance.

Face Shape and Age

Some short-faced dogs have difficulty reaching the nose with the tongue, and some older dogs develop a drier, thicker nose surface. Persistent thickening still deserves assessment because several medical conditions can look similar.

When Dryness Suggests More Than a Normal Variation

Crusting, Thickening, or Deep Cracks

A chronically rough, thickened, or crusty nose may involve excessive keratin, skin disease, infection, immune-mediated disease, or another condition. Photographs taken over several days can help show whether the surface is changing.

Bleeding, Ulcers, or Loss of Normal Texture

Bleeding spots, open sores, painful fissures, or loss of the normal cobblestone texture are reasons to schedule veterinary care. Avoid peeling crusts or scrubbing the surface.

Discharge or Sneezing

Dryness plus nasal discharge, repeated sneezing, facial swelling, or rubbing may indicate a different nasal problem. For repeated sneezing, see Why Is My Dog Sneezing So Much?.

Whole-Body Illness Signs

The nose should never be used as the only fever or hydration test. A dog that is lethargic, vomiting, not eating, weak, or behaving abnormally needs attention based on the whole clinical picture. Read Why Is My Dog Lethargic? if energy level has changed.

Is a Warm Dry Nose a Fever?

Not reliably. Nose temperature changes with sleep, room temperature, licking, and activity. A dog can have a fever with a wet nose and can be healthy with a warm dry nose. If you suspect fever or illness, a veterinarian can assess the dog properly rather than relying on nose feel.

Could It Be Dehydration?

Dehydration can occur with vomiting, diarrhea, heat exposure, reduced water intake, or illness, but a dry nose alone does not prove dehydration. Look for broader changes such as reduced energy, tacky gums, poor intake, or ongoing fluid loss. Dogs with heat-related illness, repeated vomiting, or significant diarrhea should not be managed based on the nose alone.

Safe Care at Home

  • Keep fresh water available.
  • Move bedding away from strong heat vents if the air is very dry.
  • Avoid peeling crusts or rubbing cracked areas.
  • Do not use petroleum products, essential oils, medicated human creams, or sunscreen unless your veterinarian confirms they are safe for licking.
  • Take a daily photo if you are monitoring a persistent change.

When to See a Veterinarian

Book an appointment if dryness persists and the nose becomes thick, painful, cracked, crusted, ulcerated, swollen, discolored, or bloody. Seek prompt care if the change occurs with difficulty breathing, severe lethargy, repeated vomiting, collapse, or other serious illness signs.

Related Virixoo Guides

For heat-related concerns, see How to Keep Your Dog Cool in Hot Weather. For allergy patterns involving skin and ears, read Does My Dog Have Allergies?.

Look at the Surface, Not Just the Moisture

A useful nose check is visual. Is the normal surface pattern still present? Is dryness evenly distributed or concentrated on one edge? Are there scales, crusts, cracks, ulcers, swelling, pigment loss, or a new discharge? A smooth but temporarily dry nose in a comfortable dog is much less concerning than a nose that has changed shape or texture over several weeks.

Why “Wet Nose = Healthy” Is Too Simple

Nose moisture changes quickly. A dog can wake from a nap with a warm dry nose and become wet-nosed after drinking and sniffing outside. Conversely, a sick dog may still have a wet nose. Appetite, energy, breathing, hydration, stool, urine, vomiting, pain, and behavior are much more informative when deciding whether a dog needs veterinary care.

A Dry-Nose Monitoring Checklist

CheckWhat to Note
TimingOnly after sleep, or dry all day?
TextureNormal surface, mild flakes, crusts, or deep cracks?
ColorStable pigment or new pale/pink/irregular areas?
ComfortDoes your dog rub, scratch, or avoid touch?
Whole-dog signsNormal eating, drinking, energy, breathing, and behavior?

When Photos Are Helpful

If the nose is changing slowly, take one well-lit photo each day from the same angle. This makes progression easier to see and can help your veterinarian distinguish a stable dry surface from a spreading lesion. Do not delay an appointment while collecting photos if the nose is painful, bleeding, swollen, or rapidly worsening.

FAQ

Should a healthy dog’s nose always be wet?

No. Normal nose moisture changes during the day and differs between individual dogs.

Can I put moisturizer on my dog’s dry nose?

Only use a product your veterinarian considers safe for dogs and safe if licked. Human skincare products may contain unsuitable ingredients.

Why is my dog’s nose dry after sleeping?

Dogs do not lick their noses while asleep, so temporary dryness after a nap is common.

Is a cracked nose normal?

Minor surface dryness can occur, but persistent cracking, pain, bleeding, or crusting should be examined.

Trusted References

American Kennel Club: Why Is My Dog’s Nose Dry? · PetMD: Is Dry Nose a Sign of Illness in Dogs?

title: Why Does My Dog Snore? Common Causes and When Noisy Breathing Needs a Vet
summary: Learn why dogs snore, how sleeping position, anatomy, weight, congestion and airway problems can contribute, and which breathing signs deserve veterinary attention.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Sleeping dog resting comfortably while an owner listens to gentle snoring
content:
Snoring happens when airflow becomes noisy as a dog breathes during sleep. Some dogs snore because of normal anatomy or sleeping position, while new or worsening snoring can occur with congestion, weight gain, inflammation, a foreign object, or another airway problem. The key question is whether your dog breathes comfortably while awake and asleep.

Quick Answer

If your dog has always snored lightly, sleeps comfortably, wakes normally, and has no breathing difficulty, the sound may be normal for that individual. Arrange veterinary care if snoring starts suddenly, becomes much louder, occurs with nasal discharge, coughing, exercise intolerance, restless sleep, or noisy breathing while awake. Emergency care is needed for obvious breathing difficulty, blue or gray gums, collapse, or severe distress.

What Actually Causes Snoring?

Snoring is produced when soft tissues or narrowed air passages vibrate as air moves through the nose and throat. The medical description of a low-pitched snoring sound is often “stertor.” The sound itself does not identify the cause, so timing and accompanying signs matter.

Common Reasons Dogs Snore

1. Sleeping Position

A dog lying on its back may temporarily snore more because the tongue and soft tissues shift with gravity. A neck pressed against a pillow or bed edge can also alter airflow. If the sound disappears after the dog changes position and breathing remains easy, this is generally less concerning.

2. Short-Faced Anatomy

Bulldogs, Pugs, French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, Pekingese, and other brachycephalic dogs may have narrow nostrils, an elongated soft palate, or other airway features that increase noisy breathing. Snoring may be common in these dogs, but “common” does not always mean harmless. Loud awake breathing, overheating easily, struggling with exercise, gagging, or sleep disturbance can indicate clinically important airway obstruction.

3. Nasal Congestion or Inflammation

Upper respiratory infection, environmental irritation, inflammation, or nasal discharge can narrow airflow. If snoring appears with sneezing, coughing, or a runny nose, the respiratory signs should be assessed together.

4. Weight Gain

Excess body fat can add tissue around the neck and upper airway, making airflow noisier in some dogs. Weight change should be addressed gradually with veterinary guidance, especially if the dog also tires easily or has other health conditions. See Why Is My Dog Gaining Weight?.

5. Foreign Material or a Nasal Problem

Dogs explore with their noses and can inhale plant material or debris. One-sided nasal discharge, repeated violent sneezing, pawing at the face, sudden snoring, or bleeding makes a nasal problem more important to investigate.

6. Masses, Polyps, or Other Structural Changes

Persistent progressive snoring, especially in an older dog or when accompanied by one-sided discharge or bleeding, may require imaging or further examination. These causes cannot be identified reliably from sound alone.

Snoring Versus Breathing Trouble

A sleeping dog that makes noise but has smooth chest movement and wakes normally is different from a dog working hard to breathe. Concerning breathing signs include pronounced abdominal effort, flared nostrils, extended neck, inability to settle, open-mouth breathing at rest when not hot, pale or blue gums, or collapse. For fast breathing while resting, read Why Is My Dog Breathing Fast While Resting?.

What to Observe Tonight

  1. Notice the dog’s sleeping position when snoring begins.
  2. Watch the chest and abdomen for smooth, relaxed movement.
  3. Check whether the sound stops when the dog changes position.
  4. Listen for similar noise while the dog is awake.
  5. Note nasal discharge, sneezing, coughing, gagging, or exercise intolerance.
  6. Record a short video with sound if the snoring is new or unusual.

Can You Stop a Dog From Snoring?

The answer depends on the cause. A position-related sound may improve with a different bed or posture. Weight-related airway narrowing may improve with an appropriate weight plan. Congestion or infection requires treatment of the underlying problem. Dogs with significant brachycephalic airway disease may need a veterinary airway assessment rather than home remedies.

What Not to Do

Do not give human decongestants, sleep aids, antihistamines, or cough medications unless a veterinarian has specifically recommended them. Avoid assuming that loud breathing is “just the breed” when a short-faced dog struggles in heat, exercise, or sleep.

When to Call the Vet

Schedule an appointment for new persistent snoring, worsening noise, frequent waking, nasal discharge, repeated sneezing, coughing, reduced exercise tolerance, or noisy breathing while awake. Seek urgent care for difficult breathing, blue or gray gums, collapse, severe weakness, or distress.

New Snoring Deserves More Attention Than Lifelong Snoring

A dog that has snored gently for years with no exercise or breathing problems presents a different pattern from a dog that begins snoring abruptly. New noise suggests that something changed: inflammation, congestion, weight, sleeping comfort, nasal airflow, or another airway factor. Tell your veterinarian whether the onset was sudden or gradual and whether it followed boarding, illness, trauma, dental work, or a major weight change.

Keep a One-Week Breathing Log

For seven nights, note sleeping position, snoring intensity, whether the dog wakes suddenly, and whether the noise continues after changing position. During the day, record coughing, gagging, nasal discharge, reduced stamina, heat intolerance, or noisy breathing while awake. A short recording of the sound is useful because “snoring,” “wheezing,” and “reverse sneezing” are often described differently by different people.

Snoring Patterns at a Glance

PatternWhat It Suggests
Only on the back, stops after repositioningPosition may be contributing
Longstanding in a short-faced breedAnatomy may contribute; still assess functional breathing
New snoring with sneezing or dischargeNasal or upper-airway inflammation becomes more likely
Snoring plus awake breathing noiseVeterinary airway assessment is more important
Snoring plus blue gums or collapseEmergency

FAQ

Why did my dog suddenly start snoring?

A new sound may reflect sleeping position, congestion, inflammation, weight change, or an airway problem. Sudden persistent snoring is worth discussing with a veterinarian.

Is snoring normal in Bulldogs and Pugs?

It is common, but severe or constant airway noise should not automatically be dismissed. Signs of breathing limitation deserve assessment.

Can allergies make a dog snore?

Inflammation and congestion can contribute to noisy airflow, although many conditions can produce similar signs.

Should I wake my dog if it snores?

Not for ordinary gentle snoring. Wake or seek help if breathing looks labored, the dog cannot rouse normally, or gum color is abnormal.

Trusted Reference

PetMD: What Causes Snoring in Dogs and How to Help Your Pup

title: Why Does My Dog Hump People, Dogs or Objects? Causes and How to Respond
summary: Understand why dogs hump people, other dogs or objects, how excitement, stress, play and habit contribute, and how to redirect the behavior without punishment.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Excited dog being calmly redirected by its owner away from mounting behavior
content:
Humping, also called mounting, is not automatically sexual behavior. Dogs may mount during play, excitement, stress, frustration, social interaction, or because the behavior has become a habit. Both male and female dogs can do it. The safest response is calm interruption, better management of high-arousal situations, and reinforcement of an alternative behavior.

Quick Answer

If humping happens during excitement or play, interrupt early and calmly, guide your dog to a simple alternative such as coming to you, sitting, going to a mat, or taking a short decompression break, and reward the calmer choice. Avoid yelling or physical punishment. Veterinary assessment is appropriate when mounting begins suddenly, becomes obsessive, or occurs with genital licking, urinary problems, pain, skin irritation, or other physical signs.

Why Dogs Hump

1. Excitement and Overarousal

Some dogs mount when they become too excited to regulate themselves. Guests arriving, rough play, daycare, a new dog, or intense games can raise arousal until the behavior appears. Look for what happens in the minute before the mounting rather than focusing only on the final behavior.

2. Play

Mounting can occur briefly during dog-dog play. The important issue is whether both dogs remain comfortable. A dog that repeatedly mounts another dog that is trying to leave can trigger conflict, so owners should interrupt before frustration escalates.

3. Stress or Frustration

Some dogs mount during uncertain or stressful social situations. Panting, whining, pacing, jumping, frantic movement, or difficulty responding to cues may indicate that the dog is over threshold. Reducing the intensity of the situation is often more useful than adding commands.

4. Learned Attention

If mounting reliably causes people to shout, chase, laugh, push, or engage, the behavior may gain attention value. Even negative attention can maintain a behavior in some dogs. Calmly removing access and rewarding a better behavior reduces that payoff.

5. Sexual Motivation

Hormones can contribute, especially in intact dogs, but they are not the only explanation. Neutering or spaying may reduce sexually motivated mounting in some dogs but will not necessarily erase a behavior that has become associated with excitement or habit.

6. Medical Irritation

Urinary problems, genital irritation, skin disease, or other discomfort can occasionally contribute to mounting or increased genital attention. Sudden behavior change should not be assumed to be “bad manners.”

How to Stop Humping Without Creating a Bigger Problem

Step 1: Interrupt Before Full Mounting

Learn your dog’s pre-humping pattern. Some dogs begin with intense sniffing, pawing, whining, body pressure, or frantic play. Call the dog away while they can still respond.

Step 2: Lower Arousal

Use a short calm break behind a gate, on leash near you, or in another quiet area. The goal is not punishment; it is to allow the nervous system to settle. Release the dog again when the body is loose and responsive.

Step 3: Reinforce an Alternative

Reward sitting, lying on a mat, carrying a toy, sniffing calmly, or checking in with you. The alternative should be easy enough to succeed before the dog becomes highly excited.

Step 4: Manage Repeated Triggers

If visitors reliably trigger mounting, use a leash, gate, or separate settling space before guests enter. If high-intensity dog play triggers it, choose shorter play periods and interrupt earlier. Management prevents rehearsal while new habits develop.

What If My Dog Humps Other Dogs?

Do not assume the other dog will “teach yours a lesson.” Some dogs tolerate mounting; others react strongly. Interrupt repeated mounting, create distance, and allow both dogs to calm. If your dog struggles to disengage from other dogs, reduce group play intensity and seek guidance from a qualified trainer or behavior professional.

What If My Dog Humps Guests?

Prepare before the person arrives. Use a leash or gate, provide an activity in a separate area, and reward four paws on the floor and calm orientation toward you. This approach is similar to the management used for jumping on people: prevent rehearsal, reinforce the behavior you actually want, and keep greetings manageable.

When Professional Help Is Useful

Seek veterinary advice if mounting is sudden, intense, difficult to interrupt, or accompanied by urinary changes, pain, discharge, excessive licking, or skin irritation. A qualified behavior professional can help when mounting causes fights, appears compulsive, or creates significant household problems.

Track the Trigger Before Trying to Stop the Behavior

For several days, record what happens immediately before mounting. Was there intense play? A visitor? A dog entering the room? Frustration at a barrier? Excited greeting? A favorite pillow? Also record what people do afterward. If mounting reliably creates laughter, chasing, physical play, or attention, that consequence may help maintain it. This simple observation often reveals a much clearer training target.

A Better Replacement Depends on the Trigger

TriggerUseful Alternative
Guests enteringGo to mat, chew, or calm greeting routine
Wild dog playShort break, sniffing, then lower-intensity play
Attention seekingReward sitting, toy play, or calm contact
FrustrationIncrease distance and give an achievable task
Repeated mounting of one objectTemporarily remove access while building other activities

Do Not Wait for a Fight

When another dog stiffens, turns away, hides, growls, or repeatedly tries to leave, end the interaction. Allowing one dog to continue because “they will sort it out” can turn an avoidable social mismatch into conflict. Shorter, better-managed play sessions are more useful than repeatedly letting arousal escalate.

Consistency Across the Household

Everyone should respond in the same calm way. If one person laughs and plays while another person scolds, the dog receives mixed consequences. Agree on one interruption cue, one alternative behavior, and one management plan for visitors or high-energy play. Consistency makes the replacement behavior easier to learn and reduces accidental reinforcement.

FAQ

Do female dogs hump?

Yes. Mounting occurs in both male and female dogs and can be related to excitement, play, stress, habit, or sexual behavior.

Does humping mean my dog is dominant?

It should not be reduced to a single “dominance” explanation. Context and arousal often provide more useful information.

Will neutering stop humping?

It may reduce hormonally influenced mounting in some dogs, but learned or excitement-related behavior can continue.

Should I punish my dog for humping?

No. Calm interruption, management, and reinforcement of an alternative are more useful and less likely to add stress.

Trusted Reference

American Kennel Club: Why Does My Dog Hump? Understanding Dog Humping or Mounting

title: Why Does My Dog Get the Zoomies? What FRAPs Mean and How to Keep Them Safe
summary: Dog zoomies are usually normal bursts of energy. Learn common triggers, why puppies get them, how to prevent injuries, and when frantic behavior may signal stress instead.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog get the zoomies
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Happy dog running safely across an open grassy area during a brief burst of zoomies
content:
Zoomies are usually a normal burst of high-speed activity. The behavior is often called a frenetic random activity period, or FRAP. A dog may suddenly sprint in circles, play bow, dart across a room, tuck the hindquarters, or race around for a short period before settling again. Puppies and young dogs show it most often, but adults can get zoomies too.

Quick Answer

If your dog suddenly races around for a minute or two with loose playful body language and then returns to normal, the behavior is usually harmless. Make the environment safe by moving breakable objects, avoiding slippery floors, and using a securely fenced area outdoors. Frequent frantic episodes combined with inability to settle, fear, repetitive pacing, pain, or other behavior changes deserve a closer look.

Why Dogs Get the Zoomies

Stored Energy

A dog that has been resting, confined, or waiting may release energy in one short burst. Puppies often have dramatic differences between sleep and activity, which makes their zoomies look especially intense.

Excitement

Play, seeing a favorite person, arriving at an open field, or finishing a training session can trigger a sudden burst of movement. The body is usually loose and bouncy rather than stiff or fearful.

After a Bath or Grooming

Many dogs race around after a bath. The behavior may reflect excitement, relief that handling is over, an attempt to dry off, or release of arousal. This is usually different from fear if the dog quickly returns to normal.

Evening Puppy Energy

Puppies commonly become wild in the evening when owners expect them to be tired. Sometimes the puppy truly needs an appropriate activity break; other times the puppy is overtired and losing self-control. A predictable routine with suitable play, brief training, toilet opportunities, and adequate sleep can reduce chaotic evenings.

After a Stressful Event

A dog may release built-up arousal after a veterinary visit, grooming, restraint, or another challenging event. Watch the body language during the event itself. If the dog was frightened, improving the underlying experience matters more than simply allowing more exercise afterward.

What Normal Zoomies Usually Look Like

  • Short duration.
  • Loose, curved movement.
  • Play bows or invitations to chase.
  • Normal awareness of people and surroundings.
  • Quick return to ordinary behavior.

When “Zoomies” May Be Something Else

Not every burst of movement is a FRAP. Repetitive pacing, circling that is difficult to interrupt, panic, sudden disorientation, collapse, limping, or frantic behavior with no playful body language deserves attention. A dog that repeatedly races because it cannot settle may also be under-stimulated, over-stimulated, anxious, or missing adequate rest.

How to Make Zoomies Safer

Choose Traction

Slippery tile can turn a playful sprint into a fall. Rugs, carpet, grass, or another secure high-traction area are safer than polished floors.

Clear the Route

Move sharp furniture edges, fragile objects, floor clutter, and anything the dog can crash into. Do not encourage tight high-speed circles near stairs.

Use Secure Outdoor Space

If your dog zooms outside, use a securely fenced area or another setup that prevents escape. Do not unclip a dog in an unsafe location because it “looks like it needs to run.”

Do Not Chase in a Way That Creates Risk

Some dogs interpret chasing as an invitation to run faster. If you need the dog to stop, use a practiced recall or lure the dog toward a calmer activity rather than trying to grab at full speed.

Can You Prevent Evening Zoomies?

You do not need to eliminate normal play, but routine helps. Give puppies several appropriate activity periods across the day instead of one huge exercise session. Include sniffing, short training, chewing, play, and enough sleep. Read How Much Exercise Does a Dog Need? for age-appropriate planning.

Zoomies and Sleep

Puppies and adolescent dogs can look hyperactive when they are actually overtired. If nighttime chaos is frequent, review the whole day: naps, exercise, stimulation, meals, toilet breaks, and bedtime routine. For repeated nighttime waking, see Why Does My Dog Wake Up at Night?.

When to Ask for Help

Talk with a veterinarian or qualified behavior professional if the behavior changes suddenly, becomes prolonged and repetitive, causes self-injury, appears linked to fear, or comes with limping, collapse, confusion, or other physical signs.

Zoomies Are Not a Training Failure

Owners sometimes worry that a dog racing around means obedience has disappeared. In most cases, FRAPs are simply a short burst of arousal. The useful skill is not suppressing every burst but teaching behaviors that work before and after it: recall, moving to a safe area, settling on a mat, and disengaging from dangerous spaces. Practice those skills when the dog is calm, not for the first time in the middle of a sprint.

Build a Day That Reduces Chaotic Energy

Healthy routines combine physical activity, sniffing, short training, chewing, social interaction, and rest. More exercise is not always the answer; continuously increasing intense exercise can create a dog that becomes fitter without learning to settle. Puppies in particular need substantial sleep and can become mouthy, frantic, and “wild” when overtired.

Normal Zoomies Versus a Concerning Pattern

Normal FRAPWorth Investigating
Brief and playfulLong, repetitive, hard to interrupt
Loose bodyFearful, rigid, distressed body
Returns to normal quicklyConfusion or inability to settle afterward
Occurs after excitement or restSudden new episodes with pain or neurologic signs

Use Recovery as Your Best Clue

Normal zoomies end. After the burst, the dog should be able to drink, rest, sniff, or return to ordinary interaction. If the dog remains frantic for long periods, cannot settle despite an appropriate routine, or shows repeated episodes with distress, review the pattern with a veterinarian or qualified behavior professional rather than simply adding more intense exercise.

FAQ

Are dog zoomies normal?

Yes, brief playful bursts are common, especially in puppies and young dogs.

Why does my dog get zoomies after a bath?

Excitement, relief, drying behavior, and release of arousal can all contribute.

Do zoomies mean my dog needs more exercise?

Not necessarily. Some dogs zoom despite having appropriate exercise, and overtired puppies can become more frantic rather than calmer.

Should I stop my dog’s zoomies?

You usually only need to manage safety. Interrupt if the environment is dangerous or the behavior no longer looks playful.

Trusted Reference

American Kennel Club: Why Does My Puppy Go Wild at Night?

title: Why Does My Dog Sniff Everything on Walks? Why Scent Time Matters
summary: Sniffing is a major way dogs explore the world. Learn why your dog stops to smell everything, how to balance sniffing with loose-leash walking, and when scent behavior becomes unusual.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog sniff everything on walks
secondaryKeywords: should I let my dog sniff on walks
how to stop dog sniffing everything
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog calmly sniffing grass during a relaxed leash walk with its owner
content:
Sniffing is not wasted walking time for a dog. Dogs gather enormous amounts of information through scent, so a fire hydrant, tree, patch of grass, or breeze can be as interesting to them as a busy news feed is to a person. The goal is usually not to stop sniffing but to create a walk that includes both safe scent exploration and the ability to move on when needed.

Quick Answer

Yes, it is generally beneficial to let your dog sniff during walks when the location is safe. Build predictable sniff breaks into the walk, then teach a cue such as “let’s go” for moving on. Reward your dog for checking in and walking with a loose leash between sniff opportunities. Sudden obsessive sniffing accompanied by distress, disorientation, pain, or other behavior changes should be evaluated separately.

Why Sniffing Matters So Much to Dogs

Humans rely heavily on vision; dogs rely heavily on scent. Odors can tell a dog which animals have passed through an area, whether another dog has recently urinated there, what food is nearby, and how an environment has changed since the last visit. Sniffing is therefore exploration and information gathering, not simply stubbornness.

Sniffing Can Be Mental Enrichment

A slow walk with time to investigate scents can be mentally satisfying even when it covers less distance. This does not replace appropriate physical activity, but it adds a different kind of enrichment. Some dogs appear calmer after a sniff-focused walk because they were able to engage in natural exploratory behavior.

Why Does My Dog Stop Every Few Feet?

The Area Is Scent-Rich

Popular dog-walking routes contain layers of scent from dogs, wildlife, food, people, vegetation, and weather changes. To your dog, the same sidewalk can be different every day.

Your Dog Has Learned That Pulling Reaches the Smell

If a tight leash consistently allows the dog to reach a tree or patch of grass, pulling is rewarded. You can preserve sniffing while changing how access happens: loose leash first, then permission to sniff.

Your Dog Is Anxious or Uncertain

Sniffing can sometimes appear in stressful situations. A dog may lower the head and sniff as part of displacement behavior when unsure about a person, dog, sound, or environment. Look at the entire body instead of assuming every sniff is curiosity.

A Better Walking System: Move, Sniff, Move

1. Choose a “Go Sniff” Cue

Use a phrase that means the dog has permission to explore within the leash length. This makes sniffing an intentional part of the walk.

2. Choose a Moving-On Cue

Use a separate phrase such as “let’s go.” Say it once, begin moving, and reward the dog for coming with you.

3. Reward Loose-Leash Walking With Sniffing

Sniffing itself can be the reward. Ask for several steps with a loose leash, then release the dog to investigate a safe scent. This helps the dog learn that cooperation makes access to the environment easier.

4. Pick Your Moments

Allow longer sniffing in parks, quiet sidewalks, and safe green spaces. Use shorter sniff periods near traffic, crowded areas, broken glass, discarded food, or other hazards.

What About Dogs That Pull Toward Every Smell?

Work on leash skills separately from the most distracting walk. Begin in an easier environment and reward slack in the leash. Then add controlled sniffing as a reward. See How to Leash Train a Dog Without Pulling.

When Sniffing Becomes a Safety Issue

Dogs can find discarded food, animal waste, toxic substances, medication, sharp objects, or other hazards. A reliable leave it cue is useful before the dog picks something up, while drop it is useful after an object is already in the mouth. Never allow the dog to investigate an unknown chemical, dead animal, or dangerous roadside debris closely.

Is Sniffing the Same as Sniffing Other Dogs?

The same powerful scent system is involved, but dog-to-dog investigation has additional social information. For that topic, see Why Does My Dog Sniff Other Dogs’ Rear Ends?.

When to Be Concerned

Ordinary scent exploration should be flexible: the dog can eventually move on and remains aware of the environment. Contact a veterinarian if sniffing behavior changes suddenly and occurs with confusion, persistent circling, weakness, pain, nasal bleeding, breathing changes, or other abnormal signs.

Separate “Sniff Walks” From Destination Walks

Not every outing needs the same rules. One walk can be a relaxed scent walk where the dog chooses much of the pace; another may be a practical walk where you need to reach a destination. Clear cues help the dog understand which version is happening. Predictability reduces conflict because the dog learns that moving with you does not mean sniffing opportunities disappear forever.

Use the Environment as Payment

Food rewards are useful, but the strongest reward may be the smell itself. If your dog wants a tree, ask for a few loose-leash steps and then say “go sniff.” This is a practical example of using access to what the dog wants to reinforce cooperation. Over time, the dog learns that a loose leash and check-ins help the walk continue.

A Balanced 30-Minute Walk Example

TimeActivity
First 5 minutesLoose movement and toileting
Next 10 minutesFrequent safe sniff breaks
Next 5 minutesSimple check-ins and leash practice
Next 5 minutesLonger scent exploration
Final 5 minutesCalmer return home

This is only an example. Age, health, weather, environment, and individual preference should change the plan.

FAQ

Should I let my dog sniff every walk?

Most dogs benefit from at least some safe sniffing time. The exact balance depends on the environment, training goals, and the dog.

Does sniffing tire a dog out?

It provides mental engagement and can be satisfying, but it should complement rather than replace appropriate physical exercise.

How do I stop my dog from spending five minutes at one tree?

Use a consistent moving-on cue, reward the dog for following, and offer another sniff opportunity later.

Why does my dog sniff more in a new place?

New environments contain unfamiliar scent information, so increased investigation is expected.

Trusted References

American Kennel Club: Why Does My Dog Sniff Everything? · PetMD: Why Scent Walks Are Important

title: How to Teach a Dog to Leave It: A Step-by-Step Safety Cue
summary: Teach your dog to ignore food, trash and other tempting items with a clear leave-it cue, reward-based practice and gradual real-world training.
primaryKeyword: how to teach a dog to leave it
secondaryKeywords: stop dog picking up food outside
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog calmly ignoring a treat on the floor while an owner rewards attention and self-control
content:
“Leave it” means do not take or investigate that item. It is one of the most useful safety cues you can teach because dogs encounter dropped food, medication, trash, animal waste, and unknown objects. The skill should be taught as a choice that pays well, not as a threat.

Quick Answer

Start with a treat hidden in your closed hand. Wait silently while your dog investigates. The moment the dog backs away, mark the choice and reward from your other hand. Progress to an open palm, then a protected treat on the floor, then easy real-life setups. Add the words “leave it” only after the dog understands the behavior. Never deliberately test the cue with truly dangerous objects.

Leave It Versus Drop It

The difference is important. Leave it means the dog should not pick the item up. Drop it means release something already in the mouth. Teaching both gives you a prevention cue and a backup cue. See How to Teach a Dog to Drop It after your dog understands this lesson.

What You Need

  • Small high-value treats.
  • A lower-value training treat or safe object.
  • A quiet room with few distractions.
  • A leash for later floor practice.
  • Short sessions of a few minutes.

Step 1: Closed-Fist Game

  1. Place a low-value treat inside one fist.
  2. Present the closed fist at your dog’s nose level.
  3. Say nothing while the dog sniffs, licks, or paws.
  4. The instant your dog backs the nose away, mark with “yes” or a click.
  5. Reward from the other hand, not from the leave-it hand.

This teaches a powerful rule: moving away from the temptation makes a reward appear elsewhere.

Step 2: Open-Hand Practice

Open your palm so the dog can see the treat. If the dog dives toward it, calmly close your hand. When the dog backs away, reopen. Reward from the opposite hand for ignoring the visible food. Avoid repeatedly saying “no.” Let the consequence of approaching be loss of access and the consequence of disengaging be reinforcement.

Step 3: Add the Verbal Cue

Once your dog reliably backs away as soon as the temptation appears, say “leave it” just before presenting the item. Do not repeat the words five times. One cue should predict one clear behavior.

Step 4: Treat on the Floor

Place a low-value treat on the floor and cover it with your hand or foot so the dog cannot grab it. Say the cue once. When the dog disengages, mark and reward from your hand. The floor item should remain unavailable during early practice.

Step 5: Add Distance

With the dog on leash, place an item several feet away. Walk toward it. Cue “leave it” before the leash becomes tight, reward the dog for turning toward you, then move away. Gradually decrease distance only while your dog succeeds.

Step 6: Practice With Different Safe Objects

Dogs do not automatically generalize. Practice with boring food, a toy, a tissue, a shoe, and safe household objects. Then practice outdoors with staged items you control. Never use medication, chocolate, grapes, bones, chemicals, or other dangerous material as a training test.

Step 7: Use Sniffing as a Reward

On walks, a dog may want access to a safe smell rather than food. Ask for “leave it,” reward the disengagement, then later release the dog to another safe area with a “go sniff” cue. This makes the environment part of the reinforcement system.

Common Training Mistakes

Repeating the Cue

If you say “leave it” over and over while the dog ignores you, the words lose clarity. Reduce the difficulty instead.

Making Every Temptation Too Hard

Start with something the dog can resist. Training beside discarded chicken bones on day one is not training; it is a setup for failure.

Grabbing at the Dog

Physical competition can trigger keep-away or guarding. Use management and distance so the dog cannot reach the item while learning.

Rewarding From the Forbidden Item

During early teaching, reward from a separate source. This makes disengagement clear and prevents the dog from assuming “leave it” eventually means “take the same thing.”

Using Leave It for Dogs That Eat Dirt or Grass

The cue can help interrupt unwanted ingestion but should not replace investigating persistent behavior. If your dog repeatedly eats soil, see Why Does My Dog Eat Dirt?. For grass eating, read Why Does My Dog Eat Grass?.

When to Get Training Help

If your dog guards items, snaps when approached, or has a history of swallowing dangerous objects, work with a qualified reward-based trainer or behavior professional. Resource guarding needs a careful plan rather than forced item removal. See Why Does My Dog Guard Food or Toys?.

Build Reliability With the Three Ds

Once the dog understands the basic cue, increase distance, duration, and distraction one at a time. If you move the forbidden item closer, keep the environment quiet. If you add a more exciting distraction, increase distance again. Asking for all three at once is a common reason a dog appears to “forget” a cue it actually understands.

A Four-Level Progression

LevelExample
1Treat hidden in closed fist indoors
2Visible treat on protected floor spot
3Safe object several feet away on leash
4Real walk with ordinary distractions at a manageable distance

Emergency Management Is Different From Training

If medication spills or a toxic food hits the floor, do not turn the emergency into a training test. Physically block access, move the dog behind a door or gate, and clean the hazard. Training should make future emergencies easier, but management remains part of safety even with a well-trained dog.

How to Know the Cue Is Ready for Real Life

The dog should respond on the first cue in several rooms, around different safe items, and at varying distances. Reliability means more than success with a treat in your hand. Continue to reward real-life responses generously, especially when the dog disengages from something genuinely interesting.

FAQ

How long does it take to teach leave it?

Many dogs understand the basic game quickly, but reliable real-world performance requires gradual practice across locations and distractions.

Should I say “no” before leave it?

No extra warning is required. A clear single cue is easier to understand.

Can leave it stop my dog from eating things on walks?

It can greatly improve safety, but management still matters. Use a leash, scan ahead, and avoid areas with dangerous debris.

What if my dog already has the object?

Use a separately trained “drop it” or trade cue rather than repeating “leave it.”

Trusted Reference

American Kennel Club: Leave It Command Training

title: How to Teach a Dog to Drop It: A Reward-Based Trade Method
summary: Teach your dog to release toys and safe objects on cue using trades, clear timing and positive reinforcement—without chasing, prying the mouth open or creating resource guarding.
primaryKeyword: how to teach a dog to drop it
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog releasing a toy during a calm reward-based trade exercise with its owner
content:
“Drop it” means release what is already in your mouth. The easiest way to teach it is through a fair trade: giving up an object reliably makes something good happen. This reduces chasing and conflict and can become an important safety skill when a dog picks up something inappropriate.

Quick Answer

Give your dog a low-value toy. Present a high-value treat near the nose. The moment the dog releases the toy, mark the behavior and give the treat. When safe, return the toy so the dog learns that releasing does not always end the fun. After several predictable repetitions, add the words “drop it” just before the dog releases. Gradually practice with different safe objects and distractions.

Drop It Is Not the Same as Leave It

Use leave it before the dog takes something. Use drop it after the object is in the mouth. The skills complement each other but should have separate cues. For the prevention skill, read How to Teach a Dog to Leave It.

Why Chasing Often Makes the Problem Worse

Many dogs discover that grabbing a sock makes a person run toward them. The dog then learns an exciting keep-away game. Some dogs may swallow an object when pressured because they expect it to be taken. A trade changes the emotional picture from conflict to cooperation.

Step 1: Choose the Right Practice Item

Start with a safe toy your dog likes but does not guard intensely. Do not begin with stolen food, a high-value chew, or something dangerous. Training is easier when the first decision is easy.

Step 2: Create the Trade

  1. Let the dog hold the toy for a few seconds.
  2. Bring a high-value treat to the dog’s nose.
  3. Wait for the mouth to open and the toy to fall.
  4. Mark the release immediately.
  5. Give the treat.
  6. When safe, offer the toy again.

Returning the object during practice helps prevent the dog from learning that approaching humans always means losing possessions.

Step 3: Add the Cue

When the dog predictably releases as the trade appears, say “drop it” a moment before showing the reward. After several sessions, begin saying the cue first and then rewarding the response.

Step 4: Fade the Visible Food

Keep rewards available but out of sight. Say “drop it,” wait briefly, mark the release, and then produce the reward. This prevents the food itself from becoming the only signal.

Step 5: Practice With Different Toys

Use a ball, rope toy, soft toy, and other safe items. Reward generously when moving to a more valuable object. Dogs often understand a cue in one context before they understand it everywhere.

Step 6: Add Movement and Real Life

Practice during fetch or tug. During tug, go still, ask for the release, mark it, then restart the game as the reward. In everyday situations, trade stolen safe objects rather than turning retrieval into a chase.

What If My Dog Runs Away With the Object?

Practice in a smaller room or with a leash attached to a harness under supervision so the dog cannot rehearse keep-away. Do not yank the leash to force the object out. Increase reward value and lower the value of the practice item.

What If My Dog Guards the Item?

Growling, freezing, hard staring, hovering over an object, or snapping are signs to stop informal training and get professional help. Do not punish a growl or pry the mouth open. For guarding behavior, read Why Does My Dog Guard Food or Toys?.

If the Object Is Dangerous

Training advice changes during a real emergency. If your dog has medication, a sharp object, a toxic food, or something likely to obstruct the intestine, use the safest practical trade without chasing. Contact a veterinarian or poison resource promptly when toxic ingestion is possible. Do not induce vomiting unless a veterinary professional specifically instructs you to do so.

Build a Dog Who Likes Trading

Occasionally approach your dog during normal toy play, toss a treat, and walk away without taking anything. This helps your presence predict good outcomes rather than loss. With chews, follow safe handling practices and avoid deliberately provoking guarding.

Related Virixoo Guides

For appropriate chewing outlets, see How to Choose Safe Chew Toys for Your Dog. If your dog damages household items, see How to Stop a Dog From Chewing Furniture.

Build Value for Human Approach

A dog that expects people to confiscate everything may avoid, guard, or swallow objects. During ordinary play, approach occasionally, deliver a treat, and leave the toy alone. At other times, trade and then return the item. These repetitions teach that a person approaching is not automatically bad news.

A Progression From Easy to Real Life

StagePractice
1Low-value toy, visible high-value treat
2Same toy, reward hidden until release
3Different toys and locations
4Moving games such as fetch or tug
5Safe household objects under supervision

Do Not Poison the Cue

If “drop it” always ends play, the dog may become slower to respond. During training, frequently give the toy back or immediately start another game. Save permanent removal for items that truly need to be taken away. The cue should predict a fair exchange, not automatic disappointment.

Practice Before You Need It

The worst time to discover that the cue is weak is when the dog has a dangerous object. Short easy practice several times a week creates a history of successful trades. Keep sessions calm and finish while the dog is still eager to participate.

FAQ

Should I pull an object from my dog’s mouth?

Not during routine training. Forcing the mouth can increase conflict and bite risk. Teach a voluntary release instead.

Why does my dog swallow things when I approach?

The dog may anticipate losing the item. Chasing or repeated forced removal can strengthen that pattern.

Can I use a toy instead of food as the reward?

Yes. A second toy or restarting a game can be highly effective for play-motivated dogs.

How is drop it different from leave it?

Drop it releases an item already held; leave it prevents taking the item in the first place.

Trusted Reference

American Kennel Club: How to Teach Your Dog to Drop It

title: How to Stop a Dog From Counter Surfing: Prevention and Training That Works
summary: Stop counter surfing by removing accidental rewards, managing kitchen access and teaching a strong alternative behavior while food is being prepared.
primaryKeyword: how to stop a dog from counter surfing
secondaryKeywords: stop dog jumping on kitchen counter
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog relaxing on a mat away from the kitchen counter while its owner prepares food
content:
Counter surfing is powerful because it rewards itself. A dog that finds one sandwich, crumb, or piece of meat on the counter learns that checking the surface can pay. The fastest improvement comes from making the counter consistently unrewarding while teaching the dog exactly what to do instead during meal preparation.

Quick Answer

Remove all food from reachable counters, push ingredients away from edges, use gates or supervision while cooking, and prevent the dog from practicing the behavior. At the same time, reward an alternative such as lying on a mat or staying outside the kitchen. Teach “leave it” for items the dog has not taken and “drop it” as a backup if something is already in the mouth. Avoid punishment after the food is gone; it does not undo the reward the dog already received.

Why Counter Surfing Becomes a Strong Habit

Finding food is a large reward. Even if the dog succeeds only once every twenty attempts, that unpredictable jackpot can keep checking behavior alive. This is why “mostly clean” counters often fail. Management must be consistent enough that the dog stops discovering surprise rewards.

Step 1: Make the Counter Boring

  • Store food in cabinets, containers, or the refrigerator.
  • Do not leave cooling food unattended within reach.
  • Wipe crumbs and grease from surfaces.
  • Move knives, hot pans, bones, medication, chocolate, grapes, onions, and other hazards away from edges.
  • Keep chairs and stools from becoming climbing steps for smaller dogs.

Step 2: Manage Kitchen Access

Use a gate, closed door, leash under supervision, or a defined station while you prepare food. Management is not failure; it prevents the dog from rehearsing a behavior that is highly reinforcing and potentially dangerous.

Step 3: Teach a “Place” Behavior

Choose a mat or bed a safe distance from the cooking area. Start when no food is present. Reward the dog for looking at the mat, stepping on it, lying down, and staying there briefly. Build duration gradually. Once the behavior is easy, practice while handling boring food, then normal meal preparation.

Step 4: Pay the Behavior You Want

Reward the dog for four paws on the floor, choosing the mat, or calmly staying outside the kitchen. Do not wait until the dog jumps up before offering attention. Reinforcement works best when the desired behavior becomes more profitable than checking the counter.

Step 5: Teach Leave It and Drop It

Leave it can prevent a dog from approaching a dropped item. Drop it is useful if the dog already grabbed something. These cues are safety tools, but they do not replace a clean counter and good kitchen management.

What to Do When the Dog Jumps Up

If the counter is clean, calmly guide the dog back to the floor or mat and reinforce the alternative. Avoid yelling, pushing, or creating an exciting confrontation. If food was accessible, fix the management error rather than expecting training alone to compete with a self-served meal.

Why Punishment Often Fails

Dogs may learn not to counter surf while a person is watching yet continue when alone. Punishment can also add stress or make the dog more secretive. Prevention changes what the environment teaches; reinforcement changes which behavior the dog chooses.

Counter Surfing When You Leave the Room

If the dog only steals food when unsupervised, do not test them with accessible food. Block access, clear surfaces, and use a safe area when you cannot supervise. Cameras can help confirm whether the dog is checking counters, scavenging bins, or engaging in broader separation-related behavior.

What If My Dog Begs While I Cook?

Begging and counter surfing can occur together but are not identical. For food-seeking around people, see Why Does My Dog Beg for Food?. Keep household rules consistent so one person is not rewarding behavior another person is trying to reduce.

Food Safety Matters

Counter surfing is not only inconvenient. Dogs can reach toxic foods, cooked bones, skewers, hot pans, wrappers, or medications. If your dog consumes something potentially toxic or a sharp foreign object, contact a veterinarian or animal poison service promptly rather than waiting for symptoms.

A Seven-Day Reset

  1. Clear counters completely.
  2. Set up a gate or mat station before cooking.
  3. Practice five short mat sessions without food distractions.
  4. Reward calm behavior during one easy meal-prep period each day.
  5. Prevent all unsupervised kitchen access.
  6. Practice leave it with safe staged items.
  7. Review where accidental rewards are still occurring.

Seven days will not erase every habit, but a clean streak can reveal how much the environment was maintaining the behavior.

Make the Whole Kitchen Predictable

Decide where the dog should be when food is prepared, where rewards will be delivered, and what happens when cooking ends. A mat two meters from the counter, for example, can become a clear station. If family members sometimes feed from the counter and sometimes punish the dog for approaching it, training becomes much harder.

Measure Progress by Attempts, Not Just Stolen Food

A dog may stop successfully stealing while still checking the counter fifty times a day. Track how often the dog approaches, jumps, or scans the surface. True progress means those attempts decrease because the counter has become unrewarding and the alternative behavior has become valuable.

Counter-Surfing Troubleshooting

ProblemAdjustment
Dog leaves mat every few secondsShorten duration and reward more frequently
Dog only surfs when alonePrevent unsupervised kitchen access
Dog jumps during meal prepStart mat routine before food appears
One family member feeds scrapsCreate one household rule and stick to it
Dog steals dropped itemsPractice leave it separately and manage the floor

Do Not Rely on Willpower Around Dangerous Food

Even a trained dog can make a mistake when a highly valuable item appears. Keep toxic foods and medication physically inaccessible. Training is an additional layer of safety, not permission to leave hazards within reach.

FAQ

How long does it take to stop counter surfing?

Improvement can begin quickly when access is controlled, but well-rehearsed habits may require weeks or longer of consistent management and training.

Should I use noise traps on the counter?

Start with prevention and reward-based alternatives. Startle methods can create fear and may not teach the dog what to do instead.

Why does my dog counter surf only when I leave?

The dog has probably learned that the behavior is safe and rewarding when people are absent. Prevent access rather than setting up tests.

Can small dogs counter surf?

Yes. Some climb on chairs or jump onto surfaces, so management should consider the dog’s actual reach.

Trusted Reference

American Kennel Club: How to Get Your Dog to Stop Counter-Surfing

title: Why Does My Dog Have a Runny Nose? Clear Discharge, Colored Mucus and Red Flags
summary: Learn what a runny nose in dogs can mean, why one-sided discharge matters, how color and other symptoms change urgency, and when veterinary care is needed.
primaryKeyword: why does my dog have a runny nose
secondaryKeywords: when to see vet dog runny nose
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Dog with a small amount of clear nasal discharge while an owner calmly checks its breathing
content:
A small amount of clear nasal moisture can be normal, but persistent discharge deserves context. Dogs can develop a runny nose from irritation, infection, inflammation, allergies, a foreign object, dental disease, trauma, structural problems, or other causes. The most useful details are whether discharge comes from one nostril or both, how long it lasts, what color it is, and whether the dog has sneezing, coughing, facial pain, fever-like illness signs, or breathing difficulty.

Quick Answer

If your dog has a tiny amount of clear discharge and otherwise feels normal, monitor it and keep the face clean with a soft damp cloth. Contact a veterinarian if discharge persists, becomes yellow, green, cloudy, thick, foul-smelling, or bloody; comes mainly from one nostril; or occurs with repeated sneezing, coughing, poor appetite, facial swelling, pain, or lethargy. Difficulty breathing, heavy bleeding, collapse, or severe distress requires urgent care.

What Normal Nasal Moisture Looks Like

Healthy dogs can have moisture around the nostrils because normal nasal tissues produce fluid. A brief clear drip after sniffing or exposure to cool air may not be important. Persistent discharge that wets the face, crusts around the nostril, changes color, or is accompanied by other signs is different.

Common Causes of a Runny Nose in Dogs

1. Irritation

Dust, smoke, fragrances, cleaning aerosols, dry air, and other irritants can trigger temporary nasal discharge. Remove the dog from the suspected irritant and observe whether the signs settle. Avoid strong sprays around pets.

2. Respiratory Infection

Infectious respiratory disease can produce nasal discharge along with sneezing, coughing, reduced energy, or appetite change. Dogs that have recently boarded, attended daycare, visited dog parks, or been around many unfamiliar dogs may have relevant exposure history.

3. Environmental Allergy

Allergic inflammation may contribute to clear discharge or sneezing in some dogs, but infection, irritation, and nasal disease can look similar. Do not assume every seasonal symptom is allergy without considering the whole pattern.

4. Foreign Material in the Nose

Grass awns, seeds, plant fragments, or debris can enter a nostril during sniffing. Sudden intense sneezing, pawing at the face, and discharge mainly from one nostril raise suspicion. Do not probe the nostril with tweezers or cotton swabs.

5. Dental Disease

The roots of some upper teeth lie close to the nasal cavity. Significant dental disease can contribute to nasal signs, sometimes on one side. Bad breath, difficulty chewing, facial swelling, or obvious dental disease strengthens the need for examination. See Why Does My Dog Have Bad Breath?.

6. Structural Disease or Growths

Polyps, fungal disease, trauma, or masses can cause persistent discharge. Older dogs with progressive one-sided discharge or bleeding need veterinary investigation rather than repeated home treatment.

What the Color Can Tell You—and What It Cannot

Clear fluid can occur with normal moisture, mild irritation, allergy, or early disease. Yellow or green discharge suggests inflammatory material but does not identify the exact cause. Blood may occur with trauma, a foreign body, severe inflammation, clotting problems, or a nasal lesion. Color is useful information, not a diagnosis.

One Nostril Versus Both

Discharge from both nostrils may occur with generalized respiratory or inflammatory conditions. Persistent one-sided discharge can make a local problem such as foreign material, dental disease, trauma, or a nasal lesion more important to rule out. Tell your veterinarian which side is affected.

Runny Nose With Sneezing

Sneezing is the body’s attempt to clear the nasal passages. Repeated sneezing plus discharge should be evaluated as one pattern. For a deeper guide, read Why Is My Dog Sneezing So Much?.

Runny Nose With Coughing

Coughing suggests that more than the nose may be involved. Track whether the dog was recently around other dogs and whether coughing occurs at rest, during excitement, or at night. See Why Is My Dog Coughing?.

Safe Home Care While You Monitor

  • Wipe the outside of the nose gently with a soft damp cloth.
  • Keep fresh water available.
  • Avoid smoke, strong fragrances, and aerosol cleaners.
  • Limit strenuous activity if the dog is coughing or unwell.
  • Take a photo of discharge color and a video of sneezing or breathing changes.
  • Do not put medication, oils, drops, or tools into the nostrils without veterinary direction.

When Veterinary Care Should Not Wait

Seek prompt evaluation for persistent or worsening discharge, one-sided discharge that does not resolve, blood, facial swelling, significant pain, repeated violent sneezing, poor appetite, or marked lethargy. Emergency care is appropriate for difficulty breathing, blue or gray gums, collapse, severe bleeding, or major facial trauma.

Keep Track of Duration and Direction

Two details often get forgotten: how long the discharge has been present and whether it consistently comes from the same nostril. Note the first day you observed it and check both sides in good light without inserting anything into the nose. Persistent one-sided discharge provides different diagnostic information than a brief watery discharge from both nostrils.

What a Veterinarian May Ask

Be ready to describe recent boarding or daycare, exposure to coughing dogs, plant material or tall grass, dental problems, facial trauma, medication, appetite, and energy. A photo of the discharge and a video of sneezing or breathing can be useful. Depending on the pattern, the examination may include the mouth and teeth as well as the nose and respiratory system.

Runny-Nose Pattern Guide

PatternWhy It Matters
Brief clear discharge, dog normalOften reasonable to monitor
Persistent discharge from one nostrilLocal nasal or dental causes become more important
Thick colored discharge with illness signsVeterinary evaluation is appropriate
Bloody dischargeNeeds prompt assessment, especially if recurrent
Discharge plus breathing difficultyUrgent care

Do Not Treat the Color Alone

It is tempting to assume green mucus requires a specific antibiotic or clear mucus must be allergy. Neither conclusion is reliable without examination. The same visible discharge can have different causes, so treatment should target the diagnosis rather than the color.

FAQ

Is clear nasal discharge normal in dogs?

A small temporary amount can be normal, but persistent discharge should be interpreted with the dog’s other signs.

Does green mucus always mean a bacterial infection?

No. Color alone cannot identify the exact cause and does not tell you which treatment is appropriate.

Why is only one nostril running?

A local issue such as foreign material, dental disease, trauma, or a nasal lesion becomes more important to rule out when discharge is persistently one-sided.

Can I give my dog a human decongestant?

No unless a veterinarian has specifically instructed you to use a particular medication and dose. Many human cold products can be unsafe for dogs.
